report:
## Conclusion

Yes. Strong evidence from large randomized controlled trials shows that heavy current or former smokers who undergo regular low-dose CT (LDCT) lung cancer screening have a significantly lower risk of dying from lung cancer than similar high-risk individuals who are not screened (or screened with chest X-ray).

The U.S. National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), which enrolled over 53,000 heavy smokers/ex-smokers (≥30 pack-years, current or quit within 15 years, aged 55–74), found that three rounds of annual LDCT screening reduced lung-cancer mortality by 20% compared with chest radiography, along with a 6.7% reduction in all-cause mortality (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873).

The Dutch-Belgian NELSON trial, involving over 15,000 high-risk men and women (current/former heavy smokers), used volumetric CT screening and found a 24% relative reduction in lung-cancer mortality at 10 years in men (and an even greater, though less statistically precise, reduction in women) compared with unscreened controls (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793).

These two adequately powered trials are considered the most reliable evidence base and directly informed screening guidelines. Based on this evidence, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends annual LDCT screening for adults aged 50–80 with a ≥20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years (USPSTF, https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening).

**Bottom line:** For heavy (ex-)smokers meeting risk criteria, regular LDCT screening lowers the chance of dying from lung cancer by roughly 20–24%, an effect confirmed across two major randomized trials and now the basis of national screening guidelines. Benefits must be weighed against risks like false positives, overdiagnosis, and radiation exposure, but the mortality benefit itself is well established.
